name: Cybersecurity Checklist
description: A practical security hygiene checklist for individuals and small businesses.

items.text: Use a unique, strong password for every account.
items.note: Aim for long passphrases of 12 or more characters.

items.text: Install a reputable password manager to generate and store passwords.
Turn on multi-factor authentication everywhere it is offered.
items.note: Prefer an authenticator app or security key over SMS codes.

items.text: Change any passwords you have reused across multiple sites.
Review and remove old accounts and apps you no longer use.
Check whether your email appears in known data breaches and update affected passwords.
Enable automatic updates for your operating system and apps.
Set a screen lock with a PIN, password or biometric on every device.
Turn on full-disk encryption such as BitLocker or FileVault.
Install reputable antivirus or rely on built-in protection, and keep it updated.
Enable a firewall on each computer.
Only install apps from official stores or trusted sources.
Set up remote find-and-wipe in case a device is lost or stolen.
Change the default admin password on your router.
Use WPA3 or WPA2 encryption for your Wi-Fi network.
Set a strong, unique Wi-Fi password and update it periodically.
Keep your router firmware up to date.
Create a separate guest network for visitors and smart-home devices.
Disable remote management and unused features on the router.
Identify the files and accounts you cannot afford to lose.
Follow the 3-2-1 rule: three copies, two media types, one offsite.
items.note: An offsite or cloud copy protects against theft, fire and ransomware.

items.text: Schedule automatic backups so you don't rely on memory.
Encrypt sensitive backups, especially on external drives.
Test a restore to confirm your backups actually work.
Keep at least one backup disconnected to survive ransomware.
Pause before clicking links or attachments in unexpected messages.
Verify urgent requests for money or credentials through a separate channel.
Hover over links to check the real destination before clicking.
Never share one-time codes, passwords or recovery keys with anyone.
Be cautious with public Wi-Fi and avoid logging into sensitive accounts on it.
Report suspected phishing to your provider or IT contact.
Know how to reset passwords and lock accounts quickly if compromised.
Keep account recovery information current, such as backup email and phone.
Store recovery codes for MFA in a safe, separate location.
Keep a short list of who to contact if a device or account is breached.
Review your security settings at least twice a year.

faq.q: What is the single most important cybersecurity step?
faq.a: Turning on multi-factor authentication for your important accounts. Even if a password is stolen, MFA blocks most account takeovers because the attacker also needs your phone or security key. Pair it with a unique password for every account.

faq.q: Do I really need a password manager?
faq.a: Yes. A password manager lets you use a long, unique password for every account without memorizing them. Reusing passwords is one of the most common causes of account takeover, and a manager removes that risk while making logins faster.

faq.q: How can I tell if an email is a phishing attempt?
faq.a: Watch for urgency, unexpected attachments, mismatched sender addresses and links that don't match the real site. When in doubt, don't click — go directly to the official website or app and verify the request there instead.

faq.q: Is this checklist suitable for a small business?
faq.a: Yes. The same fundamentals protect a small business and an individual. Apply them across all staff devices and accounts, and store the printable or PDF version where your team can reference it during onboarding.

faq.q: Can I download this cybersecurity checklist as a PDF?
faq.a: Yes. You can print the checklist or save it as a PDF to keep on your devices and share with family or colleagues, ticking off each habit as you secure your accounts and equipment.
